by FingerCracc

Summary

“I wanted to say thank you, I guess.”

“There’s no need for that, between us,” Mydei says, "It’s a given. I don’t stand by you for thanks.” A soft bump against his shoulder. Phainon’s head is a slight weight, his neck at an awkward angle.

“Marry me,” he says, and Mydei snorts.

“I already did.”
|
The Flame Chase is coming to an end. Mydei is still learning to be a husband and a king. He finally gets Phainon a gift.

(a duty bound epilogue)

Notes

Takes place six weeks after the end of duty bound. I would advise reading that first if you haven't already :)

Just a little note, since this is a flame reaverless/trailblazerless au, please imagine Oronyx's coreflame has already been returned and the demigod of Time is just dead at this point in the timeline like Hysilens probably is or something.

See the end of the work for more notes

chapters.title: until the sky falls
chapters.html:
The people are resentful. This much Mydei expected. They do not react well to the news he delivers, or the solution he gives them. But as their king, and their new God of Strife, it’s all Mydei can do to steer Kremnos toward toward Kephale’s light. Some go. Many are stubborn and stay.

For now, Mydei does too. He and Phainon have been organizing escort missions to allow civilians to reclaim belongings lost to the Black Tide. His soldiers spend most of their days doing this, making it as easy as possible for families to migrate. With Nikador gone, their war cries have gone quiet, and the corroded areas are safe with protection against the Black Tide creatures. Mydei leads some personally, Phainon others, but mostly the soldiers handle it and they split their time between Kremnos and Okhema. Mydei’s obligations and Phainon’s.

Now, he drags himself home with the memory of a vacant-eyed girl asking him why he’s taking her home away. Her father pulling her close and trying to explain that that’s our king, our savior, but she didn’t seem to understand at all. To her, he’s the one that gave the order to flee. He’s the one flipping her life upside down.

Krateros catches him with blood in his hair and a tired set to his expression. He claps a hand over Mydei’s shoulder. “You need a rest, Son of Gorgo,” he says, squeezing. “Leave this much to me for a while.” He doesn’t approve of Mydei’s plans either, it’s a conversation they’ve had time and time again. He wants Mydei to properly take the throne, to lead Kremnos like a real king, but he knows the black tide won’t just disappear, and he knows Mydei has long since made up his mind about ruling, and he’s accepted that. He’s a good rock, however begrudging. Mydei half smiles.

“Thank you, teacher,” he tries, “but it’s good for them to see me, if they’re going to trust that I have their best interests in mind.”

Krateros steps back, good eye softening. He might not agree, but he understands, and that’s more than enough for Mydei. “You’ve bled for them plenty, boy,” Krateros says. “They love you already. Those that don’t are stubborn and looking for someone to blame. Rest. Don’t let me catch you out for at least a day or two. I can run your missions myself without consequence.”

Mydei chuckles, wiping a bit of blood from where it crusts on his neck and makes him itch. “Won’t you be overworking yourself then?”

Krateros just shakes his head. “I’m not so willful as you not to take breaks.”

A sigh. “Alright,” Mydei agrees. He holds Krateros’ gaze. The scars on his face, the weather. He’d been a friend to Mydei’s mother. He’s a good man. “Thank you.”

“Yes, yes,” Krateros waves him off. “Go take a bath. You reek of blood.”

So Mydei heads inside the palace, up to his quarters, where he finds his husband pouring over a desk covered in papers. He looks up briefly, devoid of his usual coat and lit by warm lamplight, hair a mess. “Oh good,” he says. “You’re here. Come look at this.”

And Mydei goes despite the ache in his bones, leaning close to smell his hair. Olive oil and pine resin. He’d bathed already. A red string manifests around his finger as he points to the spread pages—maps of Kremnos, Mydei can see now. “On my patrols I found that the black tide has spread a little further.” He sweeps his finger in an arc over the fringes of the city. “All of this is gone, plus a bit of the mines. It’s like it’s moving faster now that we beat Nikador, I—”

So many things to worry about. Mydei drops his face into Phainon’s neck, closing his eyes to the warmth of him, breathing him in, nose to the center of his sun tattoo.

Phainon cuts off with an airy laugh like it tickles. He lifts a hand to Mydei’s head, trying to card through his hair before he gets stuck in tacky, bloodsoaked knots. “No wonder it smelled,” he jokes, pulling his hand away, looking at the gold that transferred to it. His skin vibrates with his voice. Mydei grunts, nips his neck. “Yeah, none of that,” Phainon says, pushing him off. “You need a bath.”

He does, desperately. He’s covered in blood, sweat, dirt. Can feel it caked to him, making him itch, making his skin crawl. And his legs feel so heavy trapped in their armor. He straightens up and struggles out of his gauntlets, leaving them with his armor racks to clean and polish later. Phainon watches him from the desk, cheek propped on his fist.

“You know,” he says. Mydei looks up from where he’s propped one leg to undo his greaves. “I don’t think you’ve said a single word since you came in.”

Mydei rolls his eyes. “Hi,” he grumbles. “Happy now?”

“So grumpy,” Phainon says, sweeping the maps into a stack, leveling the edge against the table. “That’s just like you, God of Strife.”

“Don’t call me that.” There’s a horrible racket as pieces of Mydei’s armor clang together. He’s freed one leg. Underneath, his trousers are soaked in sweat that cools in the air and gives him a chill. He wants his bath halfway to boiling.

“Alright,” Phainon says, leaving the maps behind on the desk. He stands and rolls his sleeves past his elbows, coming to stand behind Mydei, who attempts to turn his head to look at him. “Don’t move,” he says, and it’s odd but Mydei trusts him, so he doesn’t move. Phainon lifts his necklace and there’s an odd tickle in his scalp. “Your hair got stuck,” he explains. Mydei stares at his own boot, returns to shedding his armor. “I figured I’d deal with it before you decided just ripping it out was a solution.”

“I wouldn’t do that,” Mydei says. The boot comes off. Phainon gets his hair unstuck.

“Sure,” he says, letting go of the necklace, taking advantage of his position to slide his knuckles down Mydei’s spine. “And I’d even believe you if I haven’t had the misfortune of watching you comb your own hair. Really, for a Kremnoan, you’re rather unkind to it.” His fingertips land over Mydei’s weak point; he’s all too fond of touching it.

“HKS.” Mydei’s greave slips off. He steps out of it and away from Phainon, who smiles a little. He sighs through his nose. “What was it you were saying with the maps? The black tide is spreading faster?”

“I don’t think it’s productive for you to worry about that right now,” Phainon tells him, gathering Mydei’s discarding armor from the floor and setting it on the table. His hands are already covered in blood. There’s a spot beneath his jaw where Mydei had gotten it on him too. “I don’t want to stress you out more than you already are.”

“There’s no word for—”

“Stress in the Kremnoan language, yes,” Phainon finishes, cutting him off. Mydei huffs and removes the last of his plate. “I’m starting to think you’re missing more words than you have.”

“I’m taking my bath,” Mydei says, abandoning Phainon for their bath chambers, starting the water scalding and undoing his belt. Working his way out of his robes is less of an ordeal than his armor. They fall away easily as he pulls his sleeved arm free, kicking everything into a pile on the floor. As he pulls off his socks, he catches Phainon leaning against the doorframe in his peripheral, arms crossed, the trajectory of his stare less than respectful.

“Care for some company?” he asks over the roar of the water as Mydei peels himself out of his trousers. His sleeves are still rolled up, the top two buttons of his shirt undone. Mydei had left the door open on purpose.

“My eyes are up here,” he says, wetting a rag to scrub the worst of the gore away before he gets in.

Phainon lifts his gaze. “I can wash your hair for you,” he offers, as if he needs to entice Mydei somehow, as if that’s enticing. It is, but Mydei doesn’t care to admit that.

Mydei scrubs the rag over the arm he keeps bare. The difference is comical; this one is stained brown and gold, the other spared the splatter by his sleeve. “Didn’t you already bathe?” he asks. He’d smelled the soap on Phainon’s skin, suffered the ache in his teeth.

“I didn’t say I’d get in,” Phainon says. Mydei levels him with a look, dragging the cloth over his abdomen, his chest. Of course, Phainon isn’t looking at his expression. “Maybe I’ll just sit on the side and look pretty.”

Mydei snorts and tosses the rag into the pile with his clothes. He tests the water; too hot for Phainon anyway, but he’d boil himself to the brink of unconsciousness just to prove Mydei wrong if he said so. “Sure,” he says instead, reaching for a bucket of salt he keeps by the bath. A couple of handfuls go in, and he stirs the water with his hand as Phainon continues to linger.

“I was expecting more of a fight,” he notes.

Mydei straightens up and glances at him. “Why?”

A raised eyebrow. “When do you not fight me?”

“I’m quite civil, actually,” Mydei says, stepping out of his underwear too. And there’s Phainon’s wandering gaze, the way he steps out of the entryway and shuts the door.

“Civil,” he echoes as Mydei gets in. “To who, exactly?” The bath is still only half full, loud enough that they both have to raise their voices over it. He comes closer, stripping out of his shirt though his pants are far more likely to get wet if he plans to sit on the edge. His torso is a map of marks, a handful of scars and bruises, injuries from black tide creatures or his own clumsiness. His sun tattoo, that gold half circle spanning his chest. He’s worn and beautiful in a way Mydei has always kind of wished he could be too, but an immortal body bears no scars, and he has too many tattoos to have space for much else anyway.

“I wouldn’t dream of antagonizing anyone other than you,” Mydei drawls, settling in as Phainon sits as planned, passing a hand through the running water and barely hiding a flinch. His gaze flicks back to Mydei, warm like a forge or a hearth, alight with mirth.

“So I’m special, then?” he asks. The strength in his body and soul. The laugh in his voice. Mydei’s equal, in any life.

“Of course,” he says, wetting his arms, wiping at the smudges he missed. Phainon holds out a dish with a bar of soap. He takes it. “I know how much effort you put into topping my list of least favorite people.”

The red string, red glow between them. Phainon laughs, and Mydei has long since memorized the sound. “Lovely to have my efforts acknowledged,” he says. “I like to believe I’m rather adept at being a nuisance.”

“Oh, you are,” Mydei confirms, rubbing soap up his neck. The lather comes up brownish-yellow. Golden blood and dirt. He turns the water off, washes his face. When he surfaces, Phainon is still looking at him. His eyes have never really left, but right now they’re… soft, maybe.

“Lean back,” he instructs. “I’ll do your hair.”

So Mydei leans back to soak his hair through and ease the way for Phainon’s soap and fingers. He rubs the gore out, gently untangles the knots with his hands, nails over Mydei’s scalp, one hand wiping the soap from his forehead before it can drip into his eyes. Phainon is painfully gentle with this, as he always is, as an equal should be. He wouldn’t be wrong in suggesting Mydei isn’t gentle with himself. He wouldn’t be wrong in believing this a way to entice. Mydei’s eyes slip shut.

“You’re like some big cat,” Phainon tells him. “So angry on the outside, but you just want to be petted.”

Mydei could bristle at this. Should, probably, lest Phainon feel he can get away with saying such things, but he doesn’t. He’s far too tired, too aching. He’s still carrying the weight of unwanted authority. Sometimes, the hot, angry, itching sensation of Strife still fills his blood, and he isn’t used to that yet either.

“Shut up,” is all the comeback he bothers with. Phainon’s nails rake through his hair.

“Big kitty,” Phainon says.

“I hate you.”

“You know something really interesting you told me earlier?” Phainon asks. Mydei cracks an eye open, tips his head a bit to look at him, the wrinkles around his smiling eyes. “You love me, Mydeimos. Your language doesn’t even have a word for it.” A warm thrum through their string. Soap in Mydei’s hair, dripping and diffusing in the already cloudy water.

“It’s not too late to stop,” Mydei says, but Phainon just shows him one soapy hand. Red, red, red, that hangs from him and spills into the water, that connects them both.

“Oh it’s way too late,” he says, smiling so wide Mydei could almost pretend his city isn’t crumbling outside these walls, that his people aren’t angry with him, that this furious power doesn’t stick in his chest. “See this?”

“I see it,” Mydei sighs. Strife. He loves that smile. He wants to be softer than he ought to. Just for a moment. “I love you.”

“There it is,” Phainon says, a bit breathy, surprised every time Mydei says it. It’s a sticky, shallow feeling word, but it’s worth it for the way it seems to make Phainon feel. Equal is the same for Mydei, for the way it makes his chest tumble and trip over itself. “I love you too.”

“Say it,” Mydei says.

“Equal,” Phainon says, completing the trade, and Mydei is wet and covered in suds or he’d pull him down to kiss him. Instead, he stays still as Phainon fills a bowl to pour water over his head, shielding his eyes, rinsing out the soap. He lets out a low rumble, exhausted and contented in equal measure at the slip of Phainon’s fingers in his hair, freshly clean and detangled, and the heat of the bath.

“Mydei,” Phainon says after a moment, a little bit hesitant, like he’d been wanting to say this and waiting. Another bowlful of water. Mydei waits for it to stop spilling over him before he opens his eyes.

“Yes?”

Phainon reaches to refill it. “Do you think…” He stops the faucet and sets the bowl on the edge of the bath beside his thigh so he can squeeze what he can get out of Mydei’s hair. “...In another life, where things hadn’t been this way and we met each other naturally… Do you think you would still want me as your equal?”

How terribly earnest he can be. How unsure. How wretchedly feeling. “No one else can be my match the way you can. It doesn’t matter whether I want it or not, you simply are.”

He lifts the bowl now, wets his lips. “But…”

Mydei meets his gaze. This is familiar. For all his confidence and bluster, sometimes Phainon needs to be reassured and cooed at to make him feel better. Titans know where these thoughts come from. Mydei has done nothing but want him since a month after they met.

“Are you asking if I would choose you, if you hadn’t been chosen for me?” A small, tight nod. It’s difficult to say these things, but Mydei has long since learned that being equals is compromise. That love is compromise. “I certainly wouldn’t marry you quite so quickly,” he tries. Phainon doesn’t laugh, just keeps looking. Mydei clears his throat, turns back to the muddy water, “But… Yes. I believe I would.”

“Me too,” Phainon says simply, and pours that last bowl of water over him.

“Phainon.” Not HKS, not Deliverer. Mydei uses his name now, because he knows it means he’ll be more likely to take whatever happens next to heart. A soft hum is heard. Wet fingers tighten on the edge of the bath. Quit worrying, he wants to say. Stop fearing the worst. Stop thinking I don’t want you with a vengeance. What he says instead is, “You’re being an idiot.”

Phainon laughs, and it seems the message is received anyway. “I know,” he says. “You’re the overworked, exhausted one, and here I am worrying over nothing.” He sighs. “It’s always nothing. You’re wonderful, Mydei. Did you know that?”

“...Shut up.”

△

The next hour is spent meticulously cleaning and polishing his armor. Mydei finds this calming in the way he finds a bath calming. It’s the aftermath, the proof of another battle fought and won, another piece of his world protected, another moment of rest earned. Even when he was young, fresh out of the Sea of Souls, he still had to dedicate time to the upkeep of his armor. A bit of peace that didn’t cause him the same anxious, restless feeling that trying to rest does. He’d grown into being able to sit and read a book or listen to someone sing, but it had taken time and friends long lost. But this… he’s always had this.

“Do you want help?” Phainon asks as he starts, but armor is a personal thing. Mydei doesn’t know why he finds it different from letting Phainon wash his hair, but this is his blood and sweat. His responsibility. His bit of peace. He can still see that lost-looking girl, wondering why her home is being taken away from her. He rubs oil into one of his cuisses and declines, so Phainon just shrugs and returns to his maps, marking them lightly with a charcoal pencil, chewing on his cheek.

It’s clear after a while that he’s making actual calculations, actual plans relating to something about the spread of the black tide and Mydei’s homeland, Mydei’s responsibility, so Mydei takes a breath. He feels better after the bath, at least by a bit, so he allows himself to finish the polish on this piece before he says, “Tell me.”

A hum. They’re on opposite sides of the room. Phainon doesn’t turn, just asks, “Tell you what?”

“About what you’re working on,” Mydei says. “The maps. The spread of the black tide. I’ve rested enough now.”

Phainon glances at him, deliberating, gnawing on his lip. And then he stands and gathers his work before coming over and sitting with Mydei, shuffling through his papers before he finds the one he wants to display. The clean scent of him. The way he’s almost gold in this light. “There’s still blood from my hair beneath your chin,” Mydei says, but finds his fingers dirty with polish. He uses the side of his hand instead, lightly scrubbing it off, pushing Phainon’s choker askew.

“Thank you,” Phainon says, looking from his hand to his eyes, then back to the map. “Shaded in dark is what’s already lost,” he explains, pointing with the back end of his pencil. He taps some sections extending from the edges, a couple of inches from the perimeter. An inch is a massive thing, on a map. “This is what my patrol found to be corrupted today.” He pulls another page from the stack, this one covered in equations Mydei couldn’t make sense of if he tried for a week. Next, he traces a new border, a finger’s width out from the old. “I’m not done with my calculations quite yet, but I’d estimate we’ll lose about this much more within a month if it keeps spreading at this rate.”

Another wave of people, frustrated and scared and forced to flee. Hundred, thousands, even. How many will blame him? “I see.”

“We need to move more people to Okhema before it’s too late,” Phainon says. Bone weary, Mydei passes his polishing cloth over plate, studying the map, trying not to sigh.

“You think it’ll hit the market street?” he asks, eyes on that part of the map, Phainon’s markings cutting just through the end of it. A pomegranate juice stand sits just behind it, should someone walk the street in life.

“Yes,” Phainon says. “Soon. It’s spreading a bit more on the west side than the east.”

The beginnings of a headache behind his temples. “Alright.”

Phainon hesitates, breath pausing as he puts his papers back in a neat stack. Mydei swaps this piece of armor for the next. “What really needs to happen is the end of the Flame Chase,” Phainon says.

“We’re due for a trip back to Okhema,” Mydei admits. He’s been so caught up in this. His furious people. The coreflame in his chest.

“Can you really afford to leave right now?”

Mydei sighs, finishes wiping the worst of the grime away dry before he reaches for his solvent. “Krateros can handle my duties,” he says. “He’s better at delegating tasks than I am, anyway.”

“Alright,” Phainon agrees.

“Do you really believe in this ‘Era Nova?’”

“Yes,” Phainon says, easy as breathing.

“We’ll go, then.”

“Mydei.” A soft hum. Their eyes meet, and Phainon wets his lips. “I don’t know,” he says. “I wanted to say thank you, I guess.”

“For?”

“Standing by me.” But that’s just what equals are, what they do. Phainon stands with Mydei in this, Mydei stands with Phainon in the Flame Chase. They’ve had this conversation before. Their battles belong to each other.

“There’s no need for that, between us,” Mydei says, noticing that he’s grown distracted from his work cleaning his armor. He redoubles his efforts; only a couple of pieces left. He polishes them to a shine. “It’s a given. I don’t stand by you for thanks.” A soft bump against his shoulder. Phainon’s head a slight weight, his neck at an awkward angle.

“Marry me,” he says, and Mydei snorts.

“I already did,” he says, turning to glance at him, feeling the tickle of his hair. “You’re going to hurt your neck like that.”

“I want to put my mouth on you,” Phainon tells him, still in the same position, forehead on Mydei’s shoulder. It earns him nothing more than a hum as Mydei uses his nail to press his rag into the harder to clean divots of his pauldron.

“You can wait until I’m done with this,” he says. Breath down his bare arm, a sigh. “Don’t you have calculations to finish?”

“I guess so,” Phainon says, finally sitting up, shuffling through his papers again.

△

After such a long day, the bed is soft and overdue. Mydei’s armor is clean and put away, Phainon’s calculations are complete. Now, there’s a comb in his hand and his fingers in Mydei’s hair, brushing it out of the shapes it dried in, softly untangling any new or leftover knots.

“Why don’t you fight with a weapon?” Phainon sits behind him, kneeling where Mydei has his legs crossed. He’s close enough to smell, to feel the heat of, and it’s cool in Castrum Kremnos this time of year. Cooler still, when their time with the sun is coming to an end.

“I’m just more used to fighting with my hands,” Mydei explains. He’s proficient in the spear as well, passable with a sword, but he’s more in control of his own fists. They’re all he had to protect him for years. “You use a sword because that’s what you’re used to.”

“I guess so,” Phainon admits, running the comb from root to tip, finding it able to slip through smoothly, prongs skimming Mydei’s scalp. Had he been granted a normal childhood, perhaps he’d have memories like this of his mothers hands in his hair, teaching him to braid it, teaching him to start from the bottom when he brushes so he won’t push all the knots into one painful spot. As it stands, he still isn’t used to this, having someone else to care for his hair. In turn, having someone to care for him.

“It’s different, though,” Phainon continues, slipping off the bed to face Mydei instead of sitting behind him, leaving the comb in the sheets, the comb he gifted like a particularly presumptuous Kremnoan might. He steps close until his legs brush the mattress and he can collect the hair behind Mydei’s ear to braid. Terribly presumptuous. He’s long since stopped asking. “You get way more reach with a sword. You have to get in close to land any hits with just your hands.”

All this practice, and his fingers are still a little clumsy at braiding. It takes him thrice the time it takes Mydei for something a little less presentable, but there’s significance to it, implication, possession. The way Mydei wants the imprints of his teeth in Phainon’s skin, he wants Phainon to be the one to do his braid. It’s a wonderful thing, then, that he’s never had to voice that thought aloud.

“I’m good at that, though, aren’t I?”

“Well, yes,” Phainon says. “And I suppose a longer ranged opponent tends to get spooked when you get that close, flipping the advantage, but…” He frowns a little as he reaches the ends of Mydei’s hair, holding the braid in place as he scans the sheets. Mydei opens the palm of his hand to produce the cuff to secure the braid, and Phainon half smiles as he takes it.

“I can fight with a sword or a spear, you know,” Mydei says. “I’m not lacking the skill, I just prefer to use my hands.”

Phainon finishes the braid. Stands to look at him a little longer. “I guess so,” he says, gaze flicking to each of Mydei’s eyes in turn. The shirt he threw on after his bath is generously open down the front. Phainon’s eyes stray here too.

“Lecher,” Mydei scolds him.

Phainon’s stare lifts back to his. “What are you so conspicuous for, if you don’t want anyone to look?” he asks, reaching a hand out like he’s going to touch.

Mydei catches his wrist. “You’re a fool,” he says, and Phainon smiles.

“You promised me something earlier,” he says, tugging free, leaning in so they’re nose to nose. 

“Did I?” Mydei murmurs. Their mouths brush. Phainon is still smiling, so Mydei kisses it off him, craning his neck up for how standing makes Phainon taller, fisting a hand in the front of his shirt. He tastes like sweet things, fruit and milk candy that Mydei has more of a taste for than he does. One hand falls to the bed, the other finding the small of Mydei’s back, the position making him hunch a little. His breath is a contagious thing.

“There,” Mydei exhales, drifting from Phainon’s lips to his cheek, trapping skin between his teeth, gently, so gently. It would be a bad place to make a bruise. “You’ve had your mouth on me. Are you satisfied?”

Phainon’s palm on his back. His gaze is like the sun, for its heat. “Hardly,” he says, voice rough. “Scoot back.”

“And since when do I take orders from you?”

“Should I ask nicely?” Phainon tries, ducking for his neck, kissing a line from his jaw to his shoulder, fingers dipping under the hem of his shirt. At Mydei’s shaky breath, he repeats it. “Scoot back.” He sucks at a sensitive spot. “Please.”

Mydei barks a laugh, twists his hand tighter in Phainon’s shirt and uses the grip to shove him off—there’s no space for him to move otherwise. He maneuvers to the top of the bed, leaning against the pillows as Phainon crawls after him, clumsy and overeager. His legs press open, their mouths meet as Phainon settles over him, half in his lap, supporting himself with a hand on the headboard. His other hand cups Mydei’s neck, and he stops tasting sweet after Mydei kisses him one too many times. 

Living and breathing and warm, he rocks forward. Their teeth clack, and he exhales an apology as he pulls away. “Still learning,” he says, the friction a little bit painful. A dozen or more times they’ve done this; he fumbles every time but Mydei can do nothing but want him and choke on his own fondness.

“It’s fine,” Mydei tells him, groping for the drawer of his nightstand for a jar of oil. Phainon’s still touching him too much, all over, mindless, so Mydei grabs him by the chin. “Prepare me if you want this to go anywhere,” he orders and there are Phainon’s eyes like he’s in awe, like he always is, like he’s been blessed with the honor to touch, to take, when all it is is flesh, but then his gaping mouth shuts and he shakes his head.

“I wanted…” He pitches forward, lips against Mydei’s throat, warm fingers prying the jar from his and putting it back for now. “I wanted to put my mouth on you first,” he murmurs, fumbling with the ties on Mydei’s pants, unpicking the knots blind as he sucks a mark that fades in an instant. “Then… Then after, I can…”

“So get on with it,” Mydei says, batting clumsy hands away to do it himself, setting a hand on the back of Phainon’s head when he’s finished, tipping him down to look, pressing lightly, a suggestion to move lower, and Phainon does.

△

Three more days pass in Castrum Kremnos as Mydei ties up loose ends as best as he can—trusting his responsibilities to Krateros, addressing the people twice more about the spread of the black tide—and then they set off for Okhema.

Phainon advocates for passage via dromas, so that ends up being their mode of transportation. The two of them trapped in a basket, Phainon with a book on antique appraising, Mydei just watching the road. Parts of this too have been corrupted. Phainon’s ankle hooks around his. His eyes stay on the book, like this doesn’t mean a thing, and Mydei gets the urge to chew him out, though he doesn’t know what for.

A little longer. A head lands on his shoulder, Phainon adjusting the book in his hands, cheek squished when Mydei looks at him. This one section of hair sticks up on his head and threatens to tickle Mydei’s face.

“Good book?” he asks drily. The heat of their arms where they press. Mydei’s skin, Phainon’s coat.

“Hm?” Phainon hums. He looks up, twisting his cheek on Mydei’s shoulder, too close. “Well, it’s not good in the way a novel might be, but it’s been very informative.”

“And you’ve been awfully engrossed.”

The hint of a smile. “Would you rather I be distracted?” Phainon asks. He slides his bookmark in place, directing his full attention to Mydei, who wanted it and, now faced with it, doesn’t.

“No,” he says simply, because sometimes he doesn’t like the feeling in his chest, the way his heart beats too hard, flipping and climbing his throat like acid reflux. Phainon’s face is too close; he’s always too close, too comfortable with pressing into Mydei’s space like it means nothing to him at all. Maybe he’s just like that, warm and tactile as he is. It makes Mydei’s chest do stupid things.

A laugh. Phainon turns so he isn’t looking at Mydei from so close anymore, still on his shoulder, cheek smushed, hair tickling. “Suit yourself,” he says, cracking the book open again. The hand not holding it slips over Mydei’s thigh, grabbing his knee, softly testing the pads of his fingers against the spikes on his armor. “Let me know if you get bored.”

“I won’t,” Mydei tells him, eyeing the road again, dirt and trodden grass, a fringe of wildflowers.

Phainon snorts. “Won’t get bored or won’t tell me if you do?”

To that, Mydei doesn’t bother answering.

△

Okhema isn’t home, yet. Though perhaps Castrum Kremnos isn’t either. Okhema is too bright, too warm, too loud. Mydei’s life hasn’t been one full of sunshine and laughter. He feels a little bit out of place every time he comes here, but Phainon parades him around proudly with a hand around his wrist.

They get lunch in Marmoreal Market upon arrival. The two of them still get stares, months after all the fanfare of the wedding. They still catch wind of whispers, though almost all are favorable. Strange, how it could be so trivial to calm nations at odds. These people love Phainon, and now they look at Mydei and they love him too, just by association, just because they know that Phainon loves him.

He sees it in offers of free food or trinkets. A pair of orchids from a florist. Round stones of polished indigo from a girl Mydei later realizes must’ve been an immigrant from Kremnos, raised to fit in as best she can in Okhema. Because Kremnoans lionize and applaud their best, but they don’t love. Not quite the way these people do.

“I still find it strange,” Mydei says. They sit in the shade of a handful of trees as they eat souvlaki off sticks that Phainon had to argue to pay for. “The culture here.”

Phainon hums. “Yes, it’s…”

“Bright,” Mydei fills in. The weight of a gaze. He’s earned Phainon’s consideration.

“You said that before, a while ago,” he notes. “You called Okhema a ‘bright city’ and I thought you meant it literally.” A pause. He twists one of his skewers between his fingers, the meat half gone. “Is this what you meant that time?”

He’s so earnest. “Why do you remember these things?” Mydei asks.

A laugh like a candle in the dark. “I try,” Phainon tells him. “I try not to forget anything anyone tells me, just in case it’s important.”

Mydei chews a mouthful as he studies Phainon right back. Sometimes he looks tired. There aren’t many coreflames left; Mydei knows he’s destined to bear the world. The perfect vessel for it. Someone to carry life’s memories into tomorrow. “You…”

“I…?” Phainon blinks, and all Mydei can do is shake his head.

“Nothing,” he says, and takes another bite. Pushing the meat into his cheek, he adds, “Nevermind.”

“You can’t just not complete your sentences.” Phainon frowns at him. “Finish the thought.” Mydei shakes his head, chews silently. “Mydei!”

“Perhaps I was about to say something insulting and decided to spare your feelings,” Mydei offers, instead of saying I’m afraid you’ll have to carry too much. Instead of saying, if you remember everything for everyone else, what room is there for you? Instead of saying, I hope the new era will be kind to you. Because love is compromise, but Mydei still makes himself sick attempting to say these kinds of things.

Phainon’s eyebrows pinch together. He leans into Mydei’s space, too close, trying to keep him from avoiding his gaze. “Well, were you?” he asks. “What’s wrong with me, then, Mydeimos?”

“You’re much too brazen,” Mydei hisses

“I am?” Phainon laughs, incredulous. “You walk around half naked and I’m the brazen one?”

“My state of dress is perfectly normal by Kremnoan standards,” Mydei shoots back. “Even here, I’ve seen people walk around in less. If you have a problem, you can avert your eyes.”

Phainon starts to argue something back. And there, he’s swept it away, under the rug. Hopefully Phainon won’t remember and think to ask again.

△

Phainon answers Aglaea’s summons a few hours later. He’s gone for a while, and Mydei is left to his own devices. First, he takes advantage of the baths, the blessed water that chases the aches his immortal body can never quite heal on its own. He wanders the market with half a mind to shop, but buys only one thing, and has to fight like Phainon did for the right to pay for it

Later, he climbs to the rooftops to watch the people. Here, their attention can’t drown out the sound of his own thoughts.

He wonders if the people are prepared for the truth of the new era, whatever that may be. The rebirth of the dawn, whatever it means to burn away the black tide. He wonders how many of them have watched their homes crumble to ash and been forced to run, to flee to his too bright, too warm, too holy city. How many of them are his own, steered this way by his hand?

Do they like it here? Or do they feel just a little bit wrong all the time, just like Mydei does. But he’s never really had a home, not in the way most others do. Maybe that makes it easier to shift from one place to another. He’s seen the ache in Phainon’s eyes when he talks about Aedes Elysiae, felt it in the weight of his head on Mydei’s shoulder.

He sighs, and even the air is sweeter here. Cherry laurel on the breeze. The hopes of what’s left of the world packed into this one place.

“You know,” a voice says, a little bit airy from the climb up the steps, “this is not where I would have thought to find you.”

Mydei doesn’t turn. The breeze ruffles his hair, stirs his clothes against his skin. “Then why is it where you thought to check?”

Phainon chuckles. He comes to stand too close, as he always does, their shoulders near to brushing. “I looked up,” he says simply. Now, Mydei looks at him. His white hair, his golden sun, the hint of a smile playing on his lips. “Are you watching the people, or the clouds?”

“Both, I guess,” Mydei says.

“Mm.” Phainon’s gaze turns to his. Clear blue, clearer than the sky. “Well, now you’re just watching me.”

Mydei scoffs, but it’s warm in a tired way. Like nostalgia, like loving someone who says stupid things. “You embarrass us both, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

“And yet you’re the only one who’s embarrassed,” Phainon says, reaching to touch Mydei’s braid before his hand gets batted away. It makes him smile fully. “Funny how that works, Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos.”

“Hah.” Mydei looks back out at the city. The people passing by below them. Normal people, going about their lives. What would that feel like? So mundane, surely. Do they get tired of it? Do they yearn for action the way Mydei yearns for peace? “What did Aglaea want with you?”

Phainon sighs, then. The weight of the world. The Flame Chase. “We were discussing strategy,” he says. “Castorice has returned. Her journey was a success; she bears the Death coreflame now. Professor Anaxa at the Grove has… merged with Cerces. All that’s left are the coreflames of Sky and Worldbearing,” he says. He pauses, swallowing, wetting his lips. “I think I know what my destiny is now.”

“To bear the world,” Mydei breathes.

A weak laugh. “But, well… Kephale’s coreflame is already in Dawncloud. So really the only one left is Aquila’s.” He looks up, and Mydei does too. So much blue. The white of clouds. The light of the dawn device. Phainon takes a deep breath in. “Aglaea wants to conquer the sky,” he says. “Hyacine is ready. We’re so close to the Era Nova, I can almost taste it.”

“Do you mean to go with her?” Mydei asks. The slightest shift and their shoulder brush; Phainon still stands so close. “To help her take the sky.”

“Aglaea asked me to, yes,” Phainon admits. He seems guilty for this, something apologetic in his tone, his gaze directed stubbornly away when Mydei tries to meet it again. “Hyacine is no fighter, but there will be black tide creatures in her way, maybe even Aquila themself, if they’re still alive. She can’t do it alone, just the same as we couldn’t.”

“Will you have an army?”

“A small force, yes,” Phainon says. “They’ll help us clear that fortress in the sky, but after, if we have to fight the titan… Regular men are no match for the gods. It’ll be me and Hyacine, and… You, if you’re so inclined.”

“Do you really think I’d leave my equal to fight alone?”

Blazing heat in their string. Phainon’s hand wraps around his. “I’m asking, and that’s all,” he says. “I know you never wanted this to be your fight. I know you’ve only been roped in because of me, and I—”

“My entire life, all I’ve really wanted is to protect,” Mydei says. “I don’t care much for prophecies, but if you believe this Era Nova will truly usher in a new dawn, one where we won’t have to fear the black tide, then I’ll stand by you. Who knows, maybe those rays will light up the lives of my Kremnoans too, and if that’s the case, I’ll finally be able to rest.”

A chuckle. “We’re not so different, you and I.”

“You’re my equal,” Mydei reminds him. “My mirror, my match. What grander purpose would I have away from your side? Why would I leave you to fight alone against a god when you were so quick to come back when I had to do the same?”

Phainon’s fingers squeeze tight. His eyes are glassy when he smiles. “You want to do this together, then?” he asks.

It’s too late for him to turn back. It has been for a long time. Mydei’s destiny may not be his own, but he’s alright with the choices that have led him here. He’s alright with the future he’s promised. “Together,” he agrees. “Or we die trying.”

△

A body in a bed. Their sheets in Okhema are softer, woven of finer threads, steeped in a sweeter smell. Cherry laurel. Every time Mydei comes back, Krateros complains that he reeks of it. Somehow, Phainon only ever smells of pine.

“How do you feel?” Phainon asks that night, his ear pressed against Mydei’s chest. All that’s there is a heartbeat, relaxed and steady, but Phainon tries to listen like he might be able to hear the coreflame too.

“What do you mean?” Mydei asks, though he thinks he knows what he’s being asked.

“What does it feel like?” Phainon whispers, splaying his fingers across Mydei’s ribs, head lifting to look at him. “The coreflame, godhood. Does it make you feel… I don’t know. I guess I always assumed it would feel like the war cries did when we were fighting Nikador. Angry, all the time. Is it like that?”

Mydei curls a hand around one of Phainon’s wrists, devoid of his gauntlets, bare skin on bare skin. Right now, the only sensation in his chest is the hard thump of his heart, that young, stupid fluttering feeling Phainon always gives him.

Sometimes, Strife has him sick with it, fingers itching to break things. When he’s angry, he feels he could tear apart the whole world with just his teeth and his hands, but more furious is the urge to protect. His people, his nation, his… Phainon.

“I’ve gotten used to it,” he says. It isn’t quite true. Phainon’s eyes light with curiosity. His palms are warm, his gaze is warmer. “It used to sit inside my chest like a caged dog. I’d get scared I’d punch someone just for breathing wrong.”

“Really?” Now, Phainon shifts onto him more fully, one leg between his, stomach to stomach, the backs of his fingers skimming the line of Mydei’s jaw. His hand opens, presses to his cheek, thumbs over the marking beneath his eye. “But you’re so… gentle.”

“Gentle,” Mydei repeats drily. He turns his face toward Phainon’s hand, catching the pad of his thumb between his teeth.

“Mydei,” Phainon laughs.

“Never in my life have I been called gentle,” Mydei tells him, letting his thumb go, sliding both hands up Phainon’s sides under the hem of his shirt, settling on his waist. His fingers press into the muscle there, the uneven texture of scars.

“You’re capable of violence,” Phainon tells him, tracing the markings on Mydei’s throat, and giving up halfway through to lean his head back on Mydei’s chest. “But you’re not violent. I’ve seen you with children and small animals and… I don’t know, Castorice. You’re very gentle. Just look at how you’re treating me right now.”

His fingers skimming Phainon’s shoulder blades, his chin against Phainon’s hair. Gentle, maybe. It’s not a word he’s ever thought to associate with himself. The coreflame doesn’t stir in his chest, and the heart that Phainon listens to beats steadily on. Mydei pulls one hand out of his shirt to belt across his shoulders.

“Most people are gentle if those are your standards,” Mydei points out.

Phainon hums, sleepy sounding just from laying down. His hair tickles the underside of Mydei’s jaw, and he’s heavy enough to make it just a bit harder to breathe. “Maybe,” he murmurs, a scratch in his voice already. “I just don’t care much about most people when it doesn’t pertain to me.”

Mydei snorts, drags his knuckles up the dip of Phainon’s spine. “Who do you think you’re fooling?” Phainon, who remembers everything everyone tells him just in case it might be important. Phainon, who’s ready to shoulder the weight of the world just to carry everyone’s dreams into tomorrow. Phainon, who’d probably burn himself to ash if it meant he could protect a handful of smiles.

A tiny laugh. “Are you calling me selfless?” Phainon asks.

“I’m calling you self-sacrificial and idiotic.”

“Mm.” Phainon’s eyelashes tickle his chest. “You would say that.”

“Not even going to argue with me?”

Phainon is quiet for a moment. “I try not to pick battles I know I’ll lose,” he finally says, rolling to fit against Mydei’s side instead, head still on his chest, a hand slipping across his ribs. Mydei’s arm folds back around his shoulders. He’s so warm. Right now, he’s making himself so small.

“Are you falling asleep?”

“No,” Phainon answers. Red string tangled in his fingers. He prods at Mydei’s ribs a bit, tracing markings and muscle. Neither of them is particularly soft. Too many bones, too much muscle, but they do what they can to make this comfortable. Phainon’s fingers don’t help.

“Quit,” Mydei grunts. “That tickles.”

A buff of breath. Phainon’s touch grows lighter, fingertips just grazing skin, nails tracing patterns that make Mydei’s side try to flinch inward until he catches Phainon’s hand in his own. “Quit,” he says again, but Phainon just laughs, tries with his other hand even though it’s at the wrong angle, and Mydei catches that too. “Cease your assault,” Mydei tells him, and when Phainon pretends to struggle, he rolls them over, Phainon on his back, Mydei leaning over him, pinning his arms to his chest. “You’ve been beat.”

“Oh no.” Phainon pretends to swoon. “What ever will I do?” Mydei makes a face at him, letting him go and rolling off. Somehow, Phainon finds this funnier than anything else. “What?” he asks. “Didn’t you like that?”

“Shut up,” Mydei tells him, shoving his face away when he tries to get too close again. “Go back to when you were falling asleep.”

“I was never!” Phainon protests, flopping back onto the sheets, shaking the mattress, turning toward the ceiling. Sunlight shines on everything. It’s warm enough to be sticky, but Mydei misses the heat of him now that they’re only laying side by side. He folds his hands onto his stomach. Phainon does too. There’s not much to see above them, but they’re both quiet for a while. Comfortable. Comfort is an emotion Mydei would live in if he could. So little of his life has been spent in it.

“What’s your wish for the new era?” Phainon asks the ceiling.

Mydei is the one who replies, “Safety for my people.”

A hum. “And what about your wish for you?”

Comfort. The sound of Phainon’s laugh, the sight of his smile. A feeling almost like home, if he knew what that felt like. “More honest duels,” Mydei offers. “More chances to grow. More moments of quiet.”

“Sounds like a good wish,” Phainon says. When Mydei turns his head to look at him, the corners of his lips are curled, just a bit.

“And what about you?” Now, Phainon turns to look at him too. He rolls onto his side, pillowing his head on his arm.

“I want to fulfill everyone else’s wishes,” he answers first. Mydei turns toward him too, lifts an eyebrow.

“And your wish for yourself?”

Phainon hums as he thinks. He looks at Mydei, the sheets, the red string tangled between them. He inches his fingers toward it, hooks them in a couple of the coils. The string is warm and almost insubstantial, Mydei knows, but he’s able to wrap it around his fingers and palm no problem. “More days like this,” he answers after a long time. “Like the ones I had in Aedes Elysiae. Where we’re all free to roll around in bed or the wheat fields far longer than we ought to and it’s okay after.”

“You want peace,” Mydei tells him.

The hint of a smile. “Yeah,” Phainon agrees. “I guess I do. Peace and somewhere to call home.”

And really, maybe they’re not so different, the two of them. Mydei digs in his pocket for something. His one tiny purchase from the market. He presses it into Phainon’s thread tangled palm.

“What is this?” Phainon asks, turning his palm up to look. It’s a seashell. A long, pointed thing, white with marks of brown. His eyes on it are soft. He turns it in his fingers so lightly, like he might break it.

“A shell,” Mydei says, though that much is obvious. “You mentioned Aedes Elysiae was by the sea.”

“So you got me a shell.” Phainon smiles, and it’s small, slight, but the feeling in it is obvious. “I like it. Thank you.”

“It’s nothing at all,” Mydei says. “You found my mother’s signet. You got me a dozen gifts during our courtship, but I—”

“Let’s not start on that,” Phainon says. His smile shifts into something a little bit mirthful. “And in all honesty, while I did choose all of your courting gifts, Aglaea paid for most of them.” At this, Mydei barks a laugh. Phainon snorts too. “Laugh all you want,” he says. “The only one I actually paid for was the comb. And Chartonus did all the work finding your mother’s ring, I just took all the credit.”

“It was still your idea.”

“But I didn’t put myself out there too much, so I don’t want you to feel like you owe me anything. I love this, and I loved the pomegranate candies you gave me. That’s plenty.”

“I just bought the shell from a vendor,” Mydei admits. “But I made those candies. I’m glad you liked them.”

“Well, Titans,” Phainon breathes. His fingers curl around the shell and he scoots closer, sliding his other hand beneath Mydei’s neck and coming to kiss him. Just once, but it’s a long, soft thing. “Thank you,” he says.

Mydei reaches to brush hair behind his ear, but it’s too short and just falls right back out. “Equal,” he says

“Equal,” Phainon says back, smiling. “I love you.”

This one still sticks a bit in Mydei’s throat. “I love you too,” he says, completing the trade.

And there, the scrunch of Phainon’s eyes, the hint of his teeth as he smiles wider. “So gentle,” he says, teasing now. “So soft, such a sweetheart, that demigod of Strife. They say he has the bloodlust of an army, but really he’s just a big sap.”

Mydei narrows his eyes at him. “And what does that make you?”

“Ah, well,” Phainon sighs. “I guess I’m just as bad.”

△

The day passes. Mydei sleeps like the dead into the next morning. When he wakes, Phainon is already up, shirtless in front of the mirror to examine how his wounds are healing. His back is all muscles and scars, and Mydei is still half asleep, so he stays in bed and watches.

Phainon turns, craning his neck so he can see his back, and Mydei is subjected to his front. A bit of bruising around his ribs. More muscle, more scars, the gold ring tattooed across his chest. Not a single bruise left from Mydei’s teeth.

“Finally awake, are you?” he asks when he notices Mydei’s eyes are open and on him. He palms a jar of ointment from the table and approaches. “Would you help me put this on? I can’t quite reach.”

Mydei grunts. His face turns into the pillow, and Phainon chuckles. Fingers slide into his hair, combing it away from his face. “Come on,” Phainon says gently, “you were perfectly happy watching the show.”

“Tired,” Mydei mumbles. His eyes stay closed for a while before he forces them open. Phainon is still there, half clothed and waiting for him. He yawns, stretching his limbs out and resigning himself to the cruel fate of waking, because for all that they live together, sleep together, and spar together, Phainon removing his clothing is still a somewhat rare occurrence. He takes the ointment, and Phainon turns his back. There, in an odd spot above one shoulder blade is a dark bruise with a bit of scabbing at the center. It would have come from some kind of blunt scrape. Painful, probably, but Mydei doesn’t ask where it’s from.

“Why this first thing in the morning?” he asks instead, yawning again as he removes the lid on the jar.

“Well, see, Mydei, it’s not actually first thing for me. I’ve already finished reading my book, enjoyed breakfast, taken a bath…”

“Shut up,” Mydei says, smearing ointment over the injury. “It’s too early.”

When he’s done, Phainon turns to face him and bends to press a kiss to his cheek. “Thanks,” he says. “You can go back to bed now, if you want.” But Mydei wraps his arms tight around his waist and kicks him lightly in the knees to make him tumble, dragging them both back into bed, shoving his face into Phainon’s throat. “Or…” Laughter. “...Do that.”

Again, Mydei grunts, pulling them into a more comfortable position. Phainon’s hand in his hair again, lightly petting the crown of his head as his chest shakes with laughter. Their skin on skin sticks. Mydei’s hands run up Phainon’s abdomen, his bruises and scars and all his marks of strength, and he finds himself wanting profusely. His mouth gravitates toward Phainon’s warm throat.

“Remember when I said I bathed?” Phainon says, voice coming a bit flustered. His hands are pressureless on Mydei’s shoulders. “That wasn’t exactly an invitation to make me need to again.” But he offers himself up against Mydei’s lips, tilting his head to give him easier access to suck a bruise into his skin. “Every time one heals, you make a dozen more,” he adds, shaky. “It doesn’t feel fair, really. I can’t leave a single one back.”

“You braid my hair,” Mydei murmurs, because in Kremnos, it’s the most claiming thing a person can do.

Phainon’s hands find the braid behind his ear, running his fingers over it root to tip, wincing as Mydei bites him. “And how many people know that?” he asks, breathy. “Versus how many people look at my neck and know exactly what you’ve done?”

It’s a fair assessment. Possession like this is meant to be equal. Mydei licks the marks he made with his teeth. Revels in the way it makes Phainon shudder. Skin sticking, he draws back. “And what would you have me do to make it fair?”

Phainon pushes him onto his back, a hand pinning his chest. “Maybe you should start wearing something blue,” he says. “A necklace, or… earrings.” The way he looks suggesting this, smiling a little, still without his shirt. Mydei tries to pull him down to kiss him, but he’s stopped when Phainon braces himself on the pillows. “No,” he says. “You haven’t brushed your teeth.”

“Don’t want to,” Mydei grunts. He doesn’t try for a kiss again, but he presses his hips against Phainon’s between his, reaching for their pants.

“Guess I’m already covered in your slobber.” Phainon reaches to help him. “We can take that bath together, yeah?”

His smile. Mydei wants to kiss him. “Get the oil,” he says, trying to shove his pants down, pinned under Phainon’s weight.

“For me or for you?” Phainon asks, rolling off to dig it out of the bedside table. It gives Mydei the chance to kick off his pants, sending them to the floor as Phainon comes back, wriggling out of his too.

Mydei snorts. “For you, probably, if you’re asking,” he says, pulling the jar from Phainon’s fingers, already half empty. “I’m the one that likes it more, so otherwise you wouldn’t bother.”

“It’s not—” Phainon flushes a little, frowns. “It’s not like I dislike it, even if I prefer the other way,” he says, letting Mydei push him down into the sheets. “Otherwise I wouldn’t be… you know.”

“I know,” Mydei agrees. He coats his fingers in oil, pries Phainon’s legs apart. “It’s not like I’m complaining.”

△

Later, after a first bath for Mydei and a second for Phainon, they convene with Aglaea and the other Chrysos Heirs. Castorice is there, sitting alone on a bench with her hands folded in her lap. She smiles when Mydei meets her eyes, tiredly but sincerely. He gets it, he knows what it first feels like to live with a coreflame in his chest. She must still be getting used to it.

Further in the room, a man with an eyepatch is arguing with Aglaea. He speaks slowly and disdainfully, and Mydei has never seen Aglaea’s mouth pressed so thin in irritation. This must be Phainon’s famed teacher, Professor Anaxa.

Cipher is there, boredly hanging upside down from a beam in the ceiling. She smiles too when Mydei looks at her, opens one long nailed hand to wave. It’s odd because Mydei has only spoken to her once, and he was just about on the brink of death at the time.

The last in the room is a girl dressed in red with her hair in neat ringlets. Hyacine, healer and descendant of the sky folk. The soon-to-be demigod of the Sky, second to last to inherit her divinity. Her hands are clasped in front of her as she stands, and she looks terribly nervous.

“Ready to conquer the sky, Lady Hyacine?” Phainon asks her, smiling gently, coming to stand at her side. She looks at him and offers that smile back.

“About as ready as I can be,” she tries. “What about you? Are you ready to shoulder the world?”

Phainon just laughs. “Not at all,” he says. “But I’ll do it without a moment’s hesitation.”

“I see everyone has gathered,” Aglaea says, extricating herself from her conversation with Anaxa, smoothing the frustrated furrow between her brows. “I thank you all for your contributions to the Flame Chase.” A pause as she sweeps her gaze around. “That said, there is work yet to be done. The final days of our journey have come. Hyacine, step forward.”

Taking a visible breath, she does. Phainon’s hand finds Mydei’s arm, squeezing lightly.

“With only two coreflames left to return, we’ve reached the precipice of the Era Nova,” Aglaea continues. “Today, we will return Aquila’s coreflame and Hyacine will take on the authority of Sky. Tomorrow, Phainon will retrieve Kephale’s coreflame from Dawncloud, and we shall usher in the new era.”

Silence. Perhaps if they were a crowd, rather than a group of seven tired heroes, there would be cheering. Instead, a voice only scoffs. “New era my left eye.”

Aglaea glares at Anaxagoras like daggers. “But for now,” she says, “the first step.”

Phainon’s fingers tighten. Mydei pulls out of his grip to take his hand instead, squeezing back.

“Today, we take the Sky.”
